newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Defiant Netanyahu to tell U.S. no on settlement.
newsitem.headline: Defiant Netanyahu to tell U.S. no on settlement.

text.p: Israel's Benjamin Netanyahu travelled to the United States on Sunday for crisis talks with President Bill Clinton, refusing to scrap a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem that has ignited Palestinian fury.
"The construction in Jerusalem, the construction on Har Homa, will continue," the prime minister's cabinet secretary Danny Naveh told Israel army radio before they flew to the United States.
Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy expressed confidence Clinton would not demand Israel stop the 6,500-home project at Har Homa, a pine-covered hilltop which Palestinians call Jabal Abu Ghneim.

"The U.S. approach on this issue is well-known -- it does not entail confrontation or pressure, but friendly and responsible clarification, and that is the way it is going to be," Levy told reporters.
Clashes have erupted nearly every day since Israel broke ground on March 18 at the site, on land that each side claims as its own.

Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat left for India to urge Non-Aligned Movement nations "to support Palestinian political rights and condemn the Israeli settlement activity," his adviser Nabil Abu Rdainah told Reuters on Sunday.

But Israeli officials said Clinton's administration shared Israel's view that the root of the crisis was not settlements but rather the Palestinians' use of violence and "terrorism" as a political bargaining chip.
Netanyahu meets Jordan's King Hussein on Sunday in the U.S. state of Minnesota -- where the monarch had prostate surgery -- before flying to Washington to meet the president on Monday.

Netanyahu hopes to get Clinton behind his offer to seal a final peace within six months ending, if necessary, with an intensive U.S.-Israeli-PLO summit like the 1978 Camp David meeting which paved the way to Israeli-Egyptian peace.
The European Union's Middle East envoy, Miguel Angel Moratinos, has held several meetings with Israeli and Palestinian leaders in the past few days.
"Mr Moratinos has been discussing a series of confidence building measures that might be taken by both sides," said a spokesman for the envoy, declining to give details.
"He had encouraging meetings with Arafat last night and Foreign Minister Levy today," the spokesman said.

Palestinians view Netanyahu's offer of go-for-broke talks as a ploy to circumvent interim accords which already require him to hand over occupied land. They view Har Homa as a unilateral act violating a deal to negotiate the Jewish settlement issue.

It was unclear whether Netanyahu would offer Clinton a gesture to revive U.S.-backed peacemaking launched in 1993. A final deal would have to tackle the toughest issues -- Jerusalem, borders, Jewish settlers and Palestinian refugees.
U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said: "We are developing our own ideas and we're going to put them forward."
Palestinian cabinet minister Hanan Ashrawi also left for Washington on Sunday -- to present Arafat's views to U.S. administration officials on settlements and Jerusalem.
"We feel that before the American initiative is finalised in all its details, there has to be discussion with both sides -- not just with the Israeli side," she told Israeli army radio.

The Palestinians say Arafat will not negotiate with Netanyahu unless work stops on the new settlement. Israel accuses Arafat of giving a green light to suicide bombings and conditions future talks on a crackdown against "terrorism".
The Palestinian Centre for Public Opinion said on Sunday that 48.6 percent of 470 Palestinians polled backed suicide attacks against Israel as support for peace talks with the Jewish state plummets.
